story-ox.script: Picture a country fair in England, 1906, where an ox is on display and people pay sixpence to guess its weight. Francis Galton — yes, the same Galton from Class 10 — gathered nearly eight hundred tickets fully expecting to prove the crowd was foolish. But the middle guess was 1,207 pounds, and the ox actually weighed 1,198 — the crowd was off by less than one percent and beat every expert in the room. And notice this: Galton went in hoping to embarrass the crowd, yet he published the opposite result honestly. That's a random forest in one story — one guesser is a single tree, and the whole crowd is the forest.

concept-if-then-trees.script: Think of a decision tree as a model built entirely out of yes-or-no questions. You start at the top with all your data, and each question splits it in two — is the distance ten meters or less? If yes, brake; if not, ask another question, and keep going until you reach an answer at the bottom. The magic here is that you can trace exactly why the model decided anything, in plain words. Now here's a question worth arguing about: would you rather have a model that's five percent more accurate, or one that can actually tell you why it turned you down for a loan?

concept-impurity.script: So here's the whole trick behind how a decision tree thinks: it wants purity. A good question splits your group so each side leans hard toward one answer, and we measure that with something called Gini impurity — zero means perfectly clean, and around a half means it's basically a coin flip. The tree just tries every threshold on every feature, keeps the one that drops impurity the most, and repeats. Now watch this tie — two totally different questions score exactly the same gain, so which one wins is basically a coin toss, and that little bit of luck is why trees are so unstable. Hold onto that thought, because in twenty minutes it's going to explain everything.

quiz-split.script: Let's test this together. We start with 20 rows split evenly, ten BRAKE and ten GO — that's a perfect coin flip, an impurity of 0.5. Now our question sends every BRAKE to the left and every GO to the right, so each side holds just one class. Think about it: when a group is entirely one label, how impure is it? It's completely pure, zero on both sides, so the answer is 0.0 — the cleanest split you'll ever dream of, and real data almost never hands it to you.

concept-one-tree-overfits.script: Watch what happens when we let a decision tree do whatever it wants. It keeps splitting and splitting until every single leaf holds just one training example, and at that point it's perfect — 100% accurate on the data it learned from. But look at the test score: it actually gets worse, dropping to 0.778, while a shallow tree of depth three sits comfortably at 0.806. That gap between the two lines, that's overfitting made visible — the tree memorised the noise instead of the real pattern. We can fix it by pruning early, but the better fix is coming up next: don't build just one tree.

concept-forest-vote.script: Here's one of my favorite ideas in all of machine learning: a crowd of mediocre voters can beat a single expert. Imagine each voter is right just sixty percent of the time, but they vote independently — with a hundred of them, the majority is right almost ninety-eight percent of the time, because their random errors cancel out and only the signal survives. That's exactly what a random forest does: hundreds of deliberately different trees, each voting. But here's the honest catch — real trees see overlapping data, so they're not truly independent, and our forest only climbed from about 0.78 to 0.86. Still, that's free accuracy, and we keep our readability.

case-av-brake.script: Imagine a self-driving car has to decide: brake or not? Now picture a crash happens, and an investigator asks why. "The model said so" won't fly here. But a decision tree lets you print out the exact branch — speed over fifty-four, distance under fifty-eight, therefore brake — and actually argue with it. That's why safety-critical systems often ship the readable tree on purpose, even when a bigger forest scores a little higher.

Take five minutes and write one simple if-then rule you'd want a self-driving car to follow — something like "if the light is red, then stop." Here's the catch: for a car to actually learn your rule, it has to measure every part of it. "If the child looks like they might run" isn't something a car can record in a column, so it can't learn from it. Then, in pairs, try to break your own rule — when would obeying it actually be dangerous? Drop your best rule and your best counter-example in the chat.

reference-key-terms.script: Let me leave you with a handful of words worth keeping. A decision tree is just a chain of yes-or-no questions, and Gini impurity measures how mixed a group is — zero means clean, a half means a coin toss. Pruning means stopping the tree early on purpose, and an ensemble combines many models into one answer, which is where a random forest lives. Hold on to that word "ensemble" — it opens the door to almost everything you'll build later. And remember interpretability: a tree lets you follow its reasoning, while a forest quietly trades that away.

backup-boosting.script: There are two great ways to combine trees into something stronger. Bagging, like a random forest, trains lots of trees independently and lets them vote, so their random mistakes cancel out. Boosting instead builds trees one after another, each one fixing what the last got wrong. And here's the surprise: on everyday spreadsheet data, these boosted trees often beat fancy neural networks — the humble if-then tree you built tonight is still the champion.

backup-regression-trees.script: Remember that disaster from before, when a straight line confidently told us something was negative six metres tall? A regression tree simply can't make that mistake, because every prediction it gives is just an average of rows it actually saw during training. It never invents a wild value outside what it knows. But here's the catch — it has the opposite weakness. It can only ever repeat values it's already seen, in flat little steps. Every model trades one failure for another, and the real skill is choosing which flaw you can live with.
